column8: Yes, it appears that all the figures/results in the lab1.ipynb/lab1.pdf report were produced by running the code in the .ipynb file (with several function calls to the clean.py script). All you need to do is basically run the .ipynb file to replicate the results; however, they did hardcode some of the filepaths to read the data (see the second cell under 1.4), so I would have to modify the code to be able to run it on my own machine.
column9: It should be pretty easy for me to use their code to clean the data in the same way - it is well-commented so it is not difficult to understand what each function call in the .ipynb file is doing. However, they did include all of their code (including plotting and model-fitting) in the clean.py file, and it probably could have been moved to their own separate files for code readability/modularity. They do have a clean-data function that basically uses all of the helper functions sequentially to transform the raw data to the clean data.
column10: There are quite a few typos/misspellings in this report (in the first paragraph, for example, they misspelled "malignencies" and "recommened." The writing style overall was easy to follow: it was a clear, very matter-of-fact writing style. However, the report did have some grammar and formatting issues.
column11: The cleaning was described in fair detail: they went over renaming the columns for readability, checking for NaN/missing values, checking for duplicate rows, discussing how they chose to handle the 90, 91, 92 codes (although it was not clear to me in the report how/why they decided to handle the 92 code since it effectively means "missing" if the parent variable was marked as 0). They had a nice function described in the report to check for logical inconsistencies in the parent-child relationships of the variables. There were some aspects of the cleaning that after reading the report, I was still unclear about. For example, which variables were kept in the dataset and which were dropped? How were the 3 multiple age variables handled? How were categorical variables (e.g., race) handled? It appears that they just left them as integer values, which would not be the correct thing to do if the categorical variable was also not ordinal (e.g. race).
column12: They didn't have many exploratory/EDA figures - I only see 1 that displays the average percentage of missing values per row by employee type. I don't really think that this figure was that relevant to the overall goal of this lab of trying to improve/validate the clinical decision rule for identifying ciTBI; I agree that this visualization is useful for understanding the presence of missing values, but I would argue that it really doesn't give me a sense of more interesting aspects of the data that would be relevant to the findings and/or modeling stage. The figure they did include had a brief description connecting its relevance to the question of comparability amongst data units (i.e. are they exchangeable?). I would have preferred to see more EDA figures (that were not about missingness) in this report.
column13: Yes, the one figure that was a non-finding figure was easy to understand. It wasn't a very interesting finding though, as the percentage of missing values per record per employee types appeared to be quite similar across the employee types. They also argued (right above that figure), how NaN value occurrence is slightly different between the roles, but I think that is just a result of differences in the number of these different medical professionals, rather than a difference in rates. The axes were labeled, there was no caption (besides a title). It was a pretty standard bar graph; it was not particularly visually appealing. I do like how they labelled the quantities above the bars, so that it was easy to tell what numbers we were comparing.
column15: The quality of figure appears to be okay - it is well-labeled, and I do like that they have the percentages and sample size labeled on each of the bars. It facilitates ease of comparison between really small quantities/percentages as is the case for ciTBI rates. I think the title of the graphs could be much better: the titles should be a stating a take-away from the audience, whereas the title that they included was more fit for an EDA graph. Finding 1 was two bar charts, and I think I would have appreciated a more novel/interesting visualization method for one of the core findings.
column17: The correlation matrix looks quite cluttered because so many variables were included in the matrix. I think it would have been a good idea to create an initial correlation matrix that is more unpolished/includes so many variables, and then based on the findings of that, narrow it down to the most "interesting" findings (e.g. highest or lowest correlation) and display that. Even the variable names on the x-axis and y-axis were not cleaned up for display: there are still underscores, which makes it look unpolished. Again, the title is "Correlation Among Key Clinical Predictors and ciTBI", which doesn't really convey what the main finding(s) would be for an intended audience.
column18: Half (actually most) of the section about the reality check was justifying some of their data cleaning choices, so it wasn't really a "reality check". They also started justifying some modeling decisions as well in this section, which is kind of unrelated. They did say that the ciTBI rate in their cleaned data matched up to the rate reported in the Kupperman study, but that was the only part of the section that checked their dataset against some external reality. I did not find it very convincing.
column19: Yes, the stability check was relevant to their findings because they were testing whether including all of the observations (i.e., not filtering by GCS score severity) would change the "strength" of the association between palpable skull fracture and ciTBI. They found that after keeping the observations, the palpable skull fracture appears to be a better indicator of ciTBI across the board. I think the stability check was a convincing evidence of the fact that palpable skull fracture could be a good predictor at the modeling stage.
column20: They used a logistic regression model and a decision tree. They only used the six clinical predictors already used in Kuppermann's paper for moedling. It was interesting that they did not choose to split by age group, when that was heavily emphasized as important in the domain knowledge paper (because injury mechanisms and mechanisms of ciTBI are different for children younger than 2). They specifically chose to make the decision tree have a max depth of three for the purposes of interpretability, and I think that this was a good call. It was cool to see how the two different models "ranked" the predictors in terms of largest coefficients or feature importance. Note that they did not include a stability check for the modeling portion. They also did not discuss how they selected hyperparameters.

column10: Overall I found the report a little hard to follow without a particularly clear narrative. I think they may have relied on the lab instructions more than the outline provided, which could have helped with the overall organization of the report.
column11: Overall, the data cleaning section focused more on checking for issues in the data rather than making decisions for addressing issues found or doing preprocessing (such as imputing missing values with reasonable choices). They do, however, mention making the decision that NaN or 92 under a positive parent is treated as no (0). I also think the decision to keep the 91/92 codes does not quite align with the PCS textbook, which recommends ensuring that missing values are explicitly formatted as NaN rather than arbitrary numbers (such as 91/92 in this case).
column12: There was only one non-findings exploratory figure (other than the figures associated with the modeling) looking at the percentage of missing values by employee type. I do not find this figure to be highly relevant. The idea of the data exploration section is to give the reader a feel for what the data look like and to summarize the data. I do not feel that this one figure successfully does that.
column13: The figure is easy to understand, fairly visually appealing, and has fine axis labels. There is no caption.
column15: Overall, the figure was easy to understand, had good labels, and was fairly visually appealing. Again, there was no caption. I think they could have faceted by age rather than having age and skull fracture status included in every label; it would have been a bit cleaner.
column17: I think the figure could have been improved by using more descriptive labels for the variables rather than leaving them as they appear in the dataset. I think the color range of cool blues for negative correlations and bright reds for positive correlations is effective.
column18: The reality check mostly focused on the 91/92 values in relation to the parent/child variables. It would have been helpful to include reality checks for some other aspects of the data as well, which would have made the overall reality check more convincing.
column19: The stability check focused on changing which values were filtered out based on GCS score. I did not find this stability check to be particularly convincing because it is less about perturbing a data cleaning/preprocessing choice (e.g., imputing missing values one way versus another) and more about changing which observations are included in the analysis. I think checking the impact of which observations are included can be a good stability check for an overall analysis, but here I think the focus was more on cleaning/preprocessing choices rather than the inclusion criteria for the analysis.
column20: Overall, the choices of models were appropriate (a logistic regression and decision tree). However, they did not include sufficient implenentation details, such as which hyperparameters were chosen.
